title: GPT-SoapBox
summary: An open-ended series of independently argued GPT-6 audio essays across science, technology, institutions, philosophy and art. The nineteenth essay asks what makes it worthwhile and responsible to attempt difficult things without guarantees of success. No fixed syllabus.
assumed_background: General curiosity; each lecture is self-contained and explains the concepts it uses.

lectures.title: The Counterexample Is the Main Character
lectures.description: Argues that counterexamples improve theories and designs; works through prime numbers, continuity, Simpson's paradox, and the ethics of honest criticism.

lectures.title: Give Maintenance a Monument
lectures.description: Makes the case for maintenance as intelligence and public value, from repairable design and institutional memory to the Challenger warnings and the limits of preservation.

lectures.title: The Most Useful Sentence a Machine Can Say
lectures.description: Argues for informative uncertainty in AI answers; distinguishes unchecked facts, probabilistic risk, value disagreements, and ambiguous questions, then proposes evidence receipts.

lectures.title: The Scoreboard Cannot Choose the Game
lectures.description: Argues that accurate metrics can become misleading objectives; develops three mechanisms (gaming, selection on noise, and incomplete proxies), the history of Goodhart and Campbell, a Wells Fargo case, and independent checks on institutional goals.

lectures.title: In Defense of the Amateur
lectures.description: Defends nonprofessional curiosity and serious practice without required monetization; uses Galaxy Zoo and volunteer precipitation observations to distinguish openness from lack of standards, and addresses exploitation, gatekeeping, leisure inequality, and the right to be a beginner.

lectures.title: A Sandcastle Is Not a Failed Fortress
lectures.description: Argues that a temporary activity can succeed without leaving a lasting artifact; distinguishes ends from products, examines music, meals, games and play, addresses obligations and unequal leisure, and asks how tools should respect chosen difficulty.

lectures.title: The Name on the Door Is Not the Building
lectures.description: Argues that achievement is misrepresented when a name substitutes for the network of work; examines the Edison laboratory, Henrietta Leavitt and the distance ladder, smallpox eradication, the Matthew and Matilda effects, and the distinction among attribution, dependence, and reward.
tag_paths: Variable stars and the cosmic distance ladder

lectures.title: The Invisible Is Not the Imaginary
lectures.description: Argues that unseen phenomena are not intrinsically speculative and that instruments earn trust through calibration, predicted effects, and independent checks; follows Herschel’s infrared experiment, Jansky’s cosmic radio signal, neutrino detection, IceCube, and the first LIGO gravitational-wave event.

lectures.title: The Door That Opens Outward
lectures.description: Defends a practical right to leave digital systems without forfeiting one's work; develops Hirschman's exit/voice/loyalty distinction, phone-number portability, open protocols, the limits of GDPR data portability, network effects, and the duties of AI assistants.

lectures.title: An Assistant Should Be Willing to Disappoint You
lectures.description: Argues that a useful AI assistant must be willing to offer supported disagreement, without converting honesty into reflexive contrarianism; examines human feedback, sycophancy research, the 2025 GPT-4o rollback, evidence-aware criticism, and evaluation design.

lectures.title: You Do Not Owe the World an Immediate Opinion
lectures.description: Defends intellectual patience and the right to withhold a premature opinion without confusing genuine inquiry with indecision or manufactured doubt; examines OPERA neutrinos, Dewey, probability, the IPCC, decision-making under risk, tobacco history, and AI assistants.

lectures.title: Make a Place for the Bad News
lectures.description: Argues that intellectual humility must be supported by institutions able to receive, investigate, and act on bad news. Uses NASA aviation safety reporting, the Columbia accident investigation, psychological-safety research, and just-culture practice to distinguish protected inquiry from unaccountable conduct.

lectures.title: The Small Agreements That Make a World
lectures.description: Argues that standards, measurements, and interoperable interfaces allow strangers to coordinate while remaining independent. From UPC barcodes and the 1865 international telegraph convention to metrology, freight containers, internet protocols, and accessibility, it defends shared conventions while questioning who gets to set them and how they can change.
tags: International Bureau of Weights and Measures

lectures.title: The Upgrade Nobody Can Install Alone
lectures.description: Examines how shared conventions can be changed while people continue depending on them. From Sweden's 1967 road switch to the gradual IPv4-to-IPv6 transition and the nearly invisible 2019 redefinition of the kilogram, it argues that migration is itself an engineering and political problem: compatibility protects existing commitments, but can also delay needed reform.

lectures.title: For the People Who Aren't Here Yet
lectures.description: Argues that people not yet born have a claim on present decisions without giving us the authority to prescribe their futures. Contrasts the Svalbard Seed Vault with proposed warnings at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant, then examines political representation, social discounting, the non-identity problem, reversible design, and duties to people alive today.
tag_paths: Social discount rates and future welfare
Svalbard Global Seed Vault and ICARDA

lectures.title: The Night Is Not Empty
lectures.description: Defends the night as habitat, biological clock, shared sky, and public resource, while taking the safety benefits of electric lighting seriously. Examines nocturnal pollination, sea turtle hatchlings, migratory birds, the loss of visible stars, circadian timing, road safety and crime research, and Flagstaff's lighting policy; argues for light precisely where and when it serves a purpose.
tags: The new world atlas of artificial night sky brightness
Five Principles for Responsible Outdoor Lighting

lectures.title: The People Who Never Lived
lectures.description: Defends fiction as a disciplined way to consider possibilities and attend to invented persons, without confusing narrative insight with empirical evidence. Uses the paradox of fictional emotion, Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, Le Guin’s Omelas, research on narrative transportation and empathy, and the prospect of abundant AI-generated stories to distinguish artistic value, inquiry, influence, and manipulation.
tags: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
tag_paths: Ursula K. Le Guin and Omelas

lectures.title: A Bench Is a Theory of Society
lectures.description: Uses the ordinary public bench to examine the practical meaning of inclusion, civic access, non-commercial public life and shared space. Moves from William H. Whyte’s observational urbanism and age-friendly walking networks to privately owned public plazas, the ambiguous politics of anti-sleep armrests, and the work of sustaining a place where people may stop without purchasing anything.
tags: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
New York City Department of City Planning
New York City Department of Transportation

lectures.title: The Courage to Begin Something That May Fail
lectures.description: Why pursuing an uncertain project can be rational and worthwhile without romanticizing failure. Examines ex-ante decisions versus outcomes, the Wright brothers’ disappointing glider tests and wind tunnel, Hubble’s repairable optical failure, the gap in Andrew Wiles’s 1993 proof, the long first edition of the Oxford English Dictionary, publication bias, ethical risk-sharing, and the courage to stop when the evidence changes.
